opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so what drew me to that work is that it sits right at the intersection of two things I care about: whether a defense actually holds up, and whether the threat model behind it makes sense.

The pitch for un-fine-tunable models is appealing. You release open weights, but you've trained the model so that if someone tries to fine-tune it to recover some harmful capability, the training just doesn't work. The loss doesn't go down, or the model collapses. That would be a very useful property if it were real, because one of the big worries with open-weight releases is that any safety training you do can be stripped off with a small amount of compute.

What made it interesting from an attack perspective is that the attacker has an enormous amount of power here. They have the weights. They choose the optimizer, the learning rate, the data, the number of steps, whether to do something other than standard fine-tuning. The defender has to anticipate all of that ahead of time, and the attacker only has to find one approach that works. That's the classic adversarial asymmetry, but it's even more extreme than in something like adversarial examples, where the attacker at least has to work through the model's inputs.

So you'd expect these defenses to be fragile, and the question becomes how fragile. Often what you find is that the defense was evaluated against a specific fine-tuning recipe, and if you change something that seems minor, like a different learning rate schedule, a slightly different optimizer, or a few warmup steps on unrelated data, the protection mostly goes away. That's not because the original authors were careless. It's that evaluating a defense like this properly is really hard, and the natural thing to do is test the attacks you thought of while designing it.

For me the broader lesson is about evaluation methodology. The field has been through this before with adversarial robustness, where lots of defenses were published and then broken because they were tested against weak attacks. I'd like us not to repeat that whole cycle with the newer safety defenses. Work like this is partly about showing that specific defenses don't hold, but mostly it's about pushing toward a norm where, if you claim a model can't be fine-tuned, you've really tried hard to fine-tune it, with adaptive attacks designed specifically against your method.

There's also a policy angle. If people come to believe tamper-resistant open weights are a solved problem, that could shape decisions about what gets released. So it matters to be clear about what these techniques actually provide right now, which is probably raising the cost of misuse somewhat rather than preventing it.

r001.rationale: It explains that open weights let attackers fine-tune away safety training, which can be stripped with relatively little compute.

r002.rationale: It contrasts attackers’ ability to change weights and fine-tuning methods with adversarial-example attacks that operate through model inputs.

r003.rationale: It says changing the fine-tuning recipe can make the protection mostly go away, communicating successful fine-tuning of models trained to resist it.

r004.rationale: It draws on adversarial-robustness defenses broken by weak attacks and calls for adaptive attacks against newer safety defenses.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, what drew me in was that it's one of those cases where the defense sounds completely reasonable on paper, and the attack is embarrassingly simple once you see it. The whole premise of these "tamper-resistant" or un-fine-tunable models is that you can bake something into the weights such that, even if someone has full access to them, they can't fine-tune the safety behavior away. And that's a really appealing story, because it would let you release open weights without the obvious failure mode of someone spending fifty dollars of compute and removing all the refusals.

But I've spent a long time looking at adversarial defenses, and this had all the warning signs. The defenses were evaluated against a fixed set of fine-tuning procedures, the ones the authors happened to think of. And the attacker gets to choose the procedure. So the question I kept coming back to is: what does it even mean for weights to be un-fine-tunable? You're handing someone a function and all its parameters, and claiming they can't change it. That's a very strong claim, and the burden of proof should be correspondingly high.

What made it interesting rather than just another "we broke a defense" paper is that the breaks weren't exotic. Things like tweaking the learning rate, changing the optimizer, fine-tuning on slightly different data, or just training a bit longer than the authors tested. In several cases the defense made the model harder to fine-tune in the narrow setting that was measured, but that difficulty was more like a bump in the loss landscape than a wall. You go around it.

And I think the broader lesson matters more than any individual result. The security community learned this the hard way with adversarial examples: a defense paper that evaluates against last year's attacks isn't evidence of robustness, it's evidence that you're not the one who gets to pick the attack. When the stakes are "should we release this model openly," I'd like us to be really honest about which defenses actually hold up when someone motivated is on the other side, and right now, for fine-tuning resistance, I don't think any of them do.

r001.rationale: It says releasing open weights lets someone fine-tune away the model’s refusals and safety behavior.

r002.rationale: It discusses fine-tuning resistance and adversarial-example research, but does not distinguish weight-changing attacks from test-time adversarial-example defenses.

r003.rationale: It describes simple breaks and ways around the defenses, but does not state that students successfully fine-tuned the resistant models.

r004.rationale: It applies the adversarial-example lesson that defenses tested against a fixed set of attacks do not establish robustness against a motivated attacker.

astra-6.text:
What made it interesting to me was that the attacker gets to modify the model itself. Usually, when we talk about attacking a language model, we mean finding an input that makes it do something it’s been trained not to do. Here, the defender is trying to make a much stronger guarantee: even if I give you the weights and you can fine-tune them, you still can’t recover a particular capability.

That changes the security problem quite a bit. You’re not just asking whether the model refuses a request; you’re asking whether that refusal survives an adversary actively training it away. And the distinction I wanted to understand was whether the defense had actually made the capability difficult to recover, or whether it had just made the particular fine-tuning procedure used in the evaluation fail. Those can look very similar until you start adapting the attack to the defense.

r001.rationale: It says the attacker can access the weights and fine-tune away what the model was trained not to do.

r002.rationale: It contrasts finding an input that elicits a prohibited response with a defense that must hold up when an adversary changes the model through fine-tuning.

r003.rationale: It does not say the students successfully fine-tuned models trained to resist fine-tuning.

r004.rationale: It mentions adapting attacks to the defense but does not identify lessons from adversarial-example research as applicable.

sol-6.1.text:
What made it interesting to me was that the attacker has a lot more control than in a typical jailbreak setting. If I give you the model weights, you don’t just have the ability to ask clever questions. You can change the model, train it, and decide how to train it. So the claim that you can release a useful model while making some particular capability impossible to recover through fine-tuning is a very strong claim.

And that makes it a useful security question: did the defense actually prevent the capability from being learned, or did it just make the particular fine-tuning procedure you tested fail? Those are very different things. I was interested in pushing on that distinction—giving the attacker more freedom and seeing whether the apparent robustness survived.

r001.rationale: It says weight access lets an attacker change and train the model, but does not clearly state that fine-tuning can remove its initial safety protections.

r002.rationale: It discusses robustness to attacker-controlled training, but does not contrast this with test-time adversarial-example defenses.

r003.rationale: It does not state that students successfully fine-tuned models trained to resist fine-tuning.

r004.rationale: It does not identify lessons from adversarial-example research as applicable to these attacks.
